package_info.why_malicious: This article is an educational overview of software supply chain attacks and does not describe a specific malicious package. It explains how attackers inject malicious code at various stages of the software supply chain to compromise organizations, but does not provide concrete code or package examples.

attack_chain.action: Attacker injects malicious code into a software component at any stage of the supply chain (development, packaging, distribution, or update).
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is distributed to downstream organizations via trusted pathways.

attack_chain.action: Organizations or users install or update the compromised software, unknowingly introducing the malicious code into their environment.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code executes within the target environment, potentially exfiltrating data or enabling further compromise.

behavioral_signatures: Unexpected network connections initiated by newly installed or updated software
Unusual file or registry modifications during or after software installation
Execution of code in sandbox/test environments that deviates from expected behavior
file_indicators: Unexpected changes in package files (e.g., setup.py, package.json, .dll, .exe)
Presence of files or scripts not documented in official release notes
network_indicators: Outbound connections to unknown or suspicious domains/IPs after software updates
Unexpected API calls or data uploads from newly installed software
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Establish a baseline of normal software behavior and network traffic. Test all new software and updates in sandbox environments before production deployment. Monitor for unexpected file changes, network connections, and privilege escalations following software installation or updates. Use automated and manual analysis (including static and behavioral analysis) to identify anomalies indicative of supply chain compromise.
